lesson.title: From Seneca Falls to the Ballot Box: The Suffrage Movement's Long Road
lesson.summary: The campaign for women's voting rights stretched across more than seven decades, moving through splits, state-by-state victories, and finally a coordinated national push that combined lobbying with public protest.
lesson.body:
The organized fight for women's suffrage is usually traced to the Seneca Falls Convention of 1848, where Elizabeth Cady Stanton presented a Declaration of Sentiments modeled on the Declaration of Independence, listing the ways American law and custom denied women equal standing, including the right to vote. That convention grew out of the broader women's rights movement, and for the next two decades suffrage was one demand among many, often pursued alongside abolitionism.

The movement's first major split came after the Civil War, when Congress debated the Fifteenth Amendment, which barred voting discrimination based on race but said nothing about sex. Susan B. Anthony and Elizabeth Cady Stanton opposed ratifying it without also securing women's suffrage, a position that broke the wartime alliance with many abolitionists. In 1869 that disagreement split the movement into two rival organizations, Anthony and Stanton's National Woman Suffrage Association, which pushed for a federal amendment, and the American Woman Suffrage Association led by Lucy Stone, which favored a state-by-state strategy. The two groups did not reunite until 1890, when they merged into the National American Woman Suffrage Association.

In the meantime, individual states and territories moved ahead on their own. The Wyoming Territory granted women full voting rights in 1869, and when Wyoming became a state in 1890 it kept that law, becoming the first state where women could vote in all elections. Other Western states followed over the next two decades, gradually building a base of women who could vote and lobby for national change.

By the 1910s the movement had two complementary wings. Carrie Chapman Catt, who led the National American Woman Suffrage Association, pursued what she called a Winning Plan, a coordinated push for both state victories and a federal amendment. Alice Paul, who had studied militant British suffragette tactics, broke off to form the more confrontational National Woman's Party, whose members picketed the White House starting in 1917 as the Silent Sentinels and faced arrest and, in some cases, brutal treatment in jail. American women's visible contributions to the World War I effort further undercut arguments that they were unfit for full citizenship. This combination of insider lobbying and outsider pressure, built on the organizing tradition Anthony had established, pushed Congress to pass the Nineteenth Amendment in 1919 and the states to ratify it in 1920.
